paragraph.text: M2. "Suffering and death are part of nature"

being part of nature doesn't make something good or indifferent for the one who suffers. Diseases, parasites and death in childbirth are also part of human nature, and that was never a reason not to treat them. The absence of a culprit matters for judging agents, not for measuring the victims' harm.
M. Wild animals, new minds and the future ·
"That's just how nature is. Some eat others, some get sick, others die. It's part of it."
It only makes sense to speak of moral evil when there's a responsible agent.
In nature, suffering is caused by processes without intention: predation, disease, climate.
So natural suffering isn't a moral evil.
And what isn't a moral evil gives us no reason to act.
P1 and P2 are acceptable if we're talking about blame: a hurricane is guilty of nothing. The problem lies in C2, which jumps from the absence of a culprit to the absence of a victim.
: from "no one is to blame" it doesn't follow that "no one was harmed".
"Nature is cruel, that's how it is."
"Wanting to end suffering in nature is denying life."
"Natural suffering is morally neutral, because it doesn't result from choices."
"It's the circle of life." (which is C7)

Catching a cold is part of life, right? Even so, when you're sick, someone looks after you, gives you medicine and a warm drink. No one says "leave it, it's natural". What's natural can hurt just the same. And when it hurts, we help if we can.

Disease is also part of nature, and we still treat it. No one leaves a child with an infection untreated because bacteria are natural. That no one is to blame for suffering doesn't make it any less bad for the one who suffers. The question is whether we can help without causing more harm.
"If a disease is natural, would you stop treating it?"
There being an agent who chose
An arsonist is to blame; lightning isn't
There being a victim who suffered
A forest burned by lightning has as many victims as one burned by an arsonist
For the one who suffers, the origin of the suffering doesn't change what they feel.
Nature has no intentions, but animals have experiences. The suffering of an animal eaten alive by parasites isn't neutral for it.

text.bold: 2. Natural isn't a criterion of good.

paragraph.text: , John Stuart Mill observed that nature does, every day, things for which a human being would be imprisoned or hanged. Copying nature was never a good moral guide (C1).

text.bold: 3. We already intervene in the natural all the time.

paragraph.text: Vaccines, antibiotics, glasses, anaesthesia, shelter from the cold: much of civilization consists of reducing natural suffering.

Faced with an epidemic or an earthquake, no one says "it's part of nature, let's not help". The absence of a culprit was never a reason to deny help to humans. Denying it to animals for the same reason is using a criterion we apply only to them.

text.bold: 5. There's no agent, but there's someone who can help.

paragraph.text: Ethics asks not only who caused something, but also what we, who can act, ought to do.
Nature kills, tortures and destroys all the time; imitating it isn't a moral criterion

paragraph.text: Suffering matters to the one who suffers, whatever its cause

text.link: *A Journey Through Animal Ethics*, vol. VII

paragraph.text: Discusses whether natural suffering is neutral and whether nature's indifference releases us from helping
(d) The strongest counter-reply: suffering has a function

The most serious version says pain is useful: it teaches animals to avoid danger, and natural selection depends on it. Ending natural suffering would destroy something that gives meaning to animals' lives.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion
Pain serves the survival of genes, not the good of the individual. For the young animal that dies on its first day, it teaches nothing.

text.bold: We accept relieving pain that has a function.

paragraph.text: The pain of childbirth and of a fracture have functions, and we still use anaesthesia.

text.bold: No one proposes ending all pain at once.

paragraph.text: The serious proposal is to reduce avoidable suffering with research and caution (M5, M10).
M1 "Wild animals live free and happy"
When the idyllic view falls, suffering is declared natural
The same appeal, now used not to help
M3 "We didn't cause it, so we have no duty to help"
From no culprit it moves to no duty
M5 "Meddling with nature is wrong; we could make everything worse"
If it's natural, meddling would be risky
The appeal to nature returns to the plate
From the natural it concludes the acceptable
From "no one is to blame" it concludes "no one was harmed"
Measures the victim's harm by the cause's intention
Accepts treating the natural in humans, but not in animals
Earthquakes and droughts have no culprit.

text.bold: Takes their own animal to the vet.

paragraph.text: Without saying its illness "is part of it".
The natural seems good or inevitable
Not acting seems less serious than acting
Harm only seems serious when someone meant to cause it

text.link: Tomasik, "Intention-based moral reactions distort intuitions about wild animals"

paragraph.text: If suffering is part of the order of things, it seems no one is wronged by it
The principle being tested is: "suffering that's part of nature doesn't need to be relieved".
We shouldn't treat infections, cancer or malaria
Some people once said so, and lost the debate
Humanitarian aid exists precisely for this

It's right that nature isn't a moral agent and that it makes no sense to blame lions or viruses. It's also right that pain has important biological functions and that tampering with it requires great care.

But the question isn't whether nature is to blame. It's whether we, who can act, have reason to help those who suffer. And the natural origin of suffering has never, in any other context, been a reason not to help.
